content.overview: Where a company buys back its own shares out of free reserves or the securities premium account, it must transfer a sum equal to the nominal value of the shares bought back to the capital redemption reserve account and disclose the transfer in the balance sheet.
content.glance: Where a company buys back its own shares out of free reserves or the securities premium account, it must transfer a sum equal to the nominal value of the shares bought back to the capital redemption reserve account and disclose the transfer in the balance sheet.
content.study: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 69 (Transfer of certain sums to capital redemption reserve account). Where a company buys back its own shares out of free reserves or the securities premium account, it must transfer a sum equal to the nominal value of the shares bought back to the capital redemption reserve account and disclose the transfer in the balance sheet. The reserve may be applied in paying up unissued shares of the company to be issued to members as fully paid bonus shares. Do not conflate this buy-back rule with the separate capital-redemption-reserve requirements for redemption of preference shares under section 55.

sections.heading: Transfer trigger and amount
sections.body: If a company buys back its own shares out of free reserves or the securities premium account, a sum equal to the nominal value of the shares bought back must be transferred to the capital redemption reserve account.

sections.heading: Disclosure
sections.body: Details of the transfer must be disclosed in the balance sheet.

sections.heading: Permitted application
sections.body: The capital redemption reserve account may be applied in paying up unissued shares of the company to be issued to members as fully paid bonus shares.

sections.heading: Distinction from preference-share redemption
sections.body: Section 69 addresses the specified buy-back funded from free reserves or securities premium. Do not import the separate rules governing redemption of preference shares under section 55.

examples.title: Capital redemption reserve
examples.body: Where preference shares are redeemed, or buy-back is made, out of profits, a sum equal to the nominal value must be transferred to the capital redemption reserve.

hypotheticals.question: A company buys back shares using its free reserves. How much must it transfer to the capital redemption reserve?
hypotheticals.analysis: Section 69 requires a transfer equal to the nominal value of the shares bought back, with the transfer disclosed in the balance sheet.

hypotheticals.question: Can the capital redemption reserve be used for any corporate purpose?
hypotheticals.analysis: Section 69 states that it may be applied in paying up unissued shares to be issued to members as fully paid bonus shares. Do not describe it as freely distributable.

distinctions.title: Section 69 buy-back and section 55 preference-share redemption
distinctions.left: Section 69 addresses buy-back funded from free reserves or securities premium.
distinctions.right: Section 55 governs redemption of preference shares under its own conditions.

misconceptions.trap: Calculating the transfer by reference to the buy-back price rather than nominal value.
misconceptions.correction: The statutory transfer equals the nominal value of the shares bought back.

misconceptions.trap: Treating the capital redemption reserve as freely distributable or available for any purpose.
misconceptions.correction: Section 69 specifies its permitted application to paying up unissued shares for fully paid bonus shares.

misconceptions.trap: Combining section 69 buy-back rules with preference-share redemption under section 55.
misconceptions.correction: Keep section 69's buy-back trigger distinct from the separate section 55 regime.

questionsAndAnswers.question: When does section 69 require a capital redemption reserve transfer?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: When a company buys back its own shares out of free reserves or the securities premium account.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What amount is transferred?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: An amount equal to the nominal value of the shares bought back.
